newsitem.title: UK: HORSE RACING-DETTORI IN RULE BREACH BUT COLLEAGUES CLEARED.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-DETTORI IN RULE BREACH BUT COLLEAGUES CLEARED.

text.p: Twenty jockeys who failed to continue racing in October last year on what they considered dangerously heavy ground at Britain's Haydock Park were exonerated by the country's racing authorities on Thursday.

But Frankie Dettori, the man who rode an unprecedented seven winners from seven rides at Ascot last season, was found in breach of the rules for refusing to ride, although the Jockey Club, the sport's ruling body in Britain, decided to take no action against him.

Racing was abandoned at Haydock on October 16 after just one race following a course inspection by a group of senior jockeys and racing officials. Dettori expressed strong displeasure with the track's conditions.

The jockeys returned to the weighing room and shut the door, a signal interpreted as an intention not to ride, setting off one of the most controversial incidents in the Jockey Club's 250 year history. Some saw the jockeys' apparent refusal to ride as overstepping the bounds.
Eleven of the riders gave evidence in person at the two-day hearing, including the colourful Dettori, who flew in from Dubai and then dashed back to the airport before the verdict was announced.
Riders maintained the race cancellation had not been a boycott but resulted from a communication breakdown between jockeys and racing officials.
Champion jockey Pat Eddery said afterwards: "It was just an unfortunate misunderstanding. I am delighted. It was a very good decision."
A statement issued by the Jockey Club after the hearing said the committee had found that all the jockeys, with the exception of Dettori, had been prepared to ride.
"The jockeys were adamant that there had not been a 'strike' as had been reported, and the committee was satisfied there was not a collective decision to refuse to ride," it said.
"The committee did not find Mr Dettori's reason for failing to ride an acceptable one."
The racing body disputed his claim that the track was unsafe and said the decision by course stewards to continue racing had been the proper one.
But it acknowledged that proper procedures had not been entirely followed by racing officials at Haydock that day and said their actions would be reported to the disciplinary committee.
Delighted Michael Caulfield, Jockeys' Association spokesman, said: "The case is closed and it's back to work for all of us."
